extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of drama, poetry, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing and judging dramatic and poetic works, with attention to romantic vs. ancient modes, national character, endings, language, and subject-selection. Draws examples from Calderon, Shakespeare, Spenser, Milton, and national literatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of the romantic
rubrics_metrics.description: It consists entirely in that feeling of love which is predominant in the Christian religion, and through it in poetry also, by which sorrows are represented as only the way to happiness...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romanticism is rooted in Christian love and purification; it softens the tragic seriousness of ancient myth into a play of fancy. Select everything (forms, language, images) which harmonizes with this feeling of love and this play of fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian spirit and purification in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything is conceived in the spirit of this Christian love and purification, everything seen in its light, and clothed in the splendour of its heavenly colouring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that embody Christian love/purification achieve a romantic, elevated effect (example: Calderon). This spiritual interiority is a defining poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three species of dramatic termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic conclusion and representation can be of destruction, of reconciliation, and of glorification (purification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three species may appear separately or blended; authors should be aware of which termination their piece inclines toward and how intermediate steps and blendings affect the work's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence lies in internal depth of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of dramatic representation lies in the internal depth of feeling, and the hidden mysteries of the spiritual life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External technical perfection does not substitute for profound internal sentiment. Ancient models, though exemplary in form, cannot furnish universal rules for the modern higher drama because feeling differs by nation and spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: National forms and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nation must be the inventor of its own form and its own rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying one nation's rules universally; tragic and high drama are intimately connected to peculiar national feeling, so dramatists should develop forms appropriate to their own people's modes of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cold imitation of antique form
rubrics_metrics.description: The romantic is not opposed to the ancients and the antique, but to those false and frigid erudite among ourselves, who strive to imitate the form without being gifted with any portion of the enthusiasm of the antique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not copy external forms slavishly; lacking the underlying enthusiasm or sentiment makes imitation hollow and ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection of imagery and language
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to the external forms of representation and language, every thing is selected which seems most to harmonize with this feeling of love and this play of fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose images, diction, and representational modes that align with the work's emotional/spiritual centre; mismatched external colouring undermines effect (e.g., southern overflowing imagery suits its native context but may be absurd elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing of denouement — preserve doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect ... would have been very much increased by our being kept longer in doubt, had he more frequently characterized the riddle of human life with the profundity of Shakespeare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resolving mysteries too early; prolonging uncertainty increases the final impact. Calderon's fault: too quick to denouement. Conversely, Shakespeare sometimes errs by revealing the riddle without hinting the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between revealing and withholding
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare has exactly the opposite fault, of too often placing before our eyes ... the riddle of life, like a sceptical poet, without giving us any hint of the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatists should balance mystery and resolution—revealing too much or leaving matters perpetually unresolved are both faults that affect audience satisfaction and interpretive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not elevate prosaic reality to poetry on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: No true success can ever attend any attempts to raise the representation of the prosaic reality to the rank of poetry, either by means of psychological acumen, or the wit of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On stage, the purely prosaic or socially witty does not easily become poetic; prefer romantic/poetical subjects and modes rather than attempting to transmute ordinary realism into high poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study masters as specimens, not external templates
rubrics_metrics.description: He cannot be too much studied as a distant and inimitable specimen of excellence ... Least of all is the external form of the Spanish drama suitable for us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from exemplary dramatists (e.g., Calderon) at a distance—study their spirit and principles but resist wholesale copying of external forms inappropriate to your context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegory — prefer living allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: The allegory which [Spenser] has selected ... is only a dead allegory, a mere classification of all the virtues of an ethical system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory should be lively and conceal the spiritual hero under tangible adventures and events; avoid allegory that reduces characters to mere abstract classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrics reveal the poet's inner character
rubrics_metrics.description: In his lyrical pieces there breathes all the tenderness of the Idyll ... For the right understanding of his dramatic works, these lyrics are of the greatest importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short lyric pieces can disclose the dramatist's private sensibility and assist interpretation of his drama; use or study lyrics to access the author's personal feelings which may not appear directly in plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of reality and truthful depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare is the master of reality; he sets before us, with a truth that is often painful, man in his degraded state, in this corruption...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray human beings with uncompromising truth, including degradation and corruption; such truthfulness can produce deeper, more abiding effects than mere satirical railing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance satire with noble sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the midst of all the bitterness of Shakespeare, we perceive continual glimpses of thoughts and recollections more pure than satirists partake in; meditation on the original height and elevation of man ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when employing satirical or bitter depiction, retain moments of lofty, tender sentiment—this contrast enriches the work and prevents mere cynicism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience and theatrical tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare regarded the drama as entirely a thing for the people, and at first treated it throughout as such ... whatever enlargements and improvements he introduced ... were all calculated and conceived according to the peculiar spirit of his predecessors and of the audience in London.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft dramatic works with awareness of popular reception and the theatrical traditions of your audience; innovations should be intelligible and resonant with that audience's spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive reliance on a single great model
rubrics_metrics.description: They [Shakespeare's writings] are indeed, in themselves, most highly poetical, but they are far from being the only poetical ones, and the dramatic art may attain perfection in many other ways besides the Shakespearian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat any single master (e.g., Shakespeare) as the sole model; explore diverse paths to dramatic excellence and adapt multiple influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness in Christian epic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The loss of Paradise forms in itself no complete whole, but is only the first act of the great Christian history of man, wherein the creation, the fall, and the redemption, are all equally necessary parts of one mighty drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating grand Christian mythic themes, include the full arc (creation, fall, redemption) to form a complete epic drama; partial treatments may feel structurally deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance linguistic standards with native mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: Any exclusive standard is injurious in a language composed of opposite elements as the English is; it is the very nature of such a language ... to retain the freedom of approximating more nearly at different times to the two opposite boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imposing a single prescriptive standard (e.g., too Latinizing or too Teutonic) on a mixed language; leverage its capacity to vary between elements for poetic richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject selection for epic and national suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Had a French poet chosen some part of the ancient national history to be the groundwork of an epic poem ... The achievements and fortunes of St. Lewis might ... have appeared the best subject of an epic poem for a poet of old France.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose epic subjects that align with national history, legend, or spiritual temperament; avoid ill-suited or artificial foundations (e.g., building a national epic on an absurd or remote legend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between stylistic perfection and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: It is true there is much reason to wish that, along with this skilful perfection, a little more freedom had been left ... It might have been quite possible to unite ... the perfection of a rich and earnest style with the poetical spirit of chivalry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for technical and stylistic excellence (e.g., polished diction, versification) while preserving poetic freedom and the romantic spirit; excessive regulation of language can curtail imaginative range.
